questions.question: What does 'git merge' do, and what is the difference between fast-forward and 3-way merge?
questions.title: git merge: Fast-Forward vs 3-Way Merge
questions.direct_answer: git merge integrates changes from one branch into another; a fast-forward merge simply moves the branch pointer forward when there's a linear history, while a 3-way merge creates a new merge commit when histories have diverged.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how branches get integrated and what merge commits are
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing what a merge commit is or why it has two parent commits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention '--no-ff' flag to force a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible, preserving branch history

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: git merge combines the history of one branch into another. There are two scenarios. In a fast-forward merge, your feature branch was created from main, you made some commits on the feature branch, but nobody made any commits on main in the meantime. Since the history is linear, Git can just move the main branch pointer forward to the tip of the feature branch — no merge commit needed. It's as if you made those commits directly on main. In a 3-way merge, both main and the feature branch have new commits since they diverged — they've gone in different directions. Git has to look at three points: the common ancestor, the tip of main, and the tip of the feature branch, and combine them. The result is a new merge commit that has two parents — one from each branch. This merge commit records the fact that two lines of history were joined. You can force Git to always create a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible with 'git merge --no-ff', which many teams prefer because it explicitly shows that a feature branch was merged.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Fast-forward merge: linear history, no new commits — branch pointer just advances; no merge commit
3-way merge: diverged histories — Git finds common ancestor and creates a merge commit with two parents
A merge commit is a special commit with two parent commits
'git merge --no-ff' forces a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible
Use 'git merge feature-branch' while on the target branch (e.g., main)

questions.question: What is git rebase and how does it work?
questions.title: git rebase Explained
questions.direct_answer: git rebase moves or replays a series of commits on top of another base commit, creating a linear history without merge commits — it rewrites commit history by creating new commit objects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of one of Git's most powerful but potentially dangerous operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that rebase rewrites commits (creates new SHA hashes) — which is why it's dangerous on shared branches
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain interactive rebase (-i) for squashing, reordering, and editing commits

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: git rebase takes the commits from your current branch and replays them one by one on top of another branch. Imagine you branched off main at commit A, made commits B and C on your feature branch, and meanwhile main got commits D and E. If you rebase your feature branch onto main, Git takes your commits B and C, temporarily sets them aside, fast-forwards your branch to match main (now at E), and then replays B and C on top. The result is a linear history that looks like you made B and C after D and E, with no merge commit. This is cleaner and easier to read. The trade-off is that rebase technically rewrites history — your commits B and C get new SHA hashes because their parent commit changed. This is why there's a golden rule with rebase: never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch that others are working on. If you do, their history will diverge from yours and things get messy. Safe use: rebase your local feature branch onto an updated main before opening a pull request.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, creating a linear history
Avoids merge commits — history appears as if development was always linear
Rewrites commit history — your commits get new SHA hashes
Golden rule: NEVER rebase commits already pushed to a shared/public branch
'git rebase -i' (interactive) allows squashing, reordering, and editing commits in the rebase

questions.question: When should you use git merge vs git rebase?
questions.title: Merge vs Rebase: When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: Use merge to preserve the true history of how branches evolved (safe for shared branches); use rebase to create a clean, linear history (only on local/private branches before pushing).

interviewer_intent.testing: Judgment and trade-off awareness — this is a classic interview question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying one is always better than the other without acknowledging the context and team conventions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that many teams use 'squash and merge' on GitHub as a middle ground

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The merge-vs-rebase debate is really about trade-offs, and honest teams will tell you neither is universally better. Merge preserves the true history — you can see exactly when branches diverged and merged, who worked on what feature, and merge commits record that context. This is valuable for auditing and understanding a complex codebase. The downside is that in active repositories the history becomes a complex graph of merge commits that's hard to read. Rebase creates a linear, clean history where every commit reads like a clear progression. It's easier to follow with 'git log --oneline'. The downside is that it rewrites commit hashes, which is a problem on shared branches. The practical answer most teams land on: rebase locally to keep your feature branch up to date with main and to clean up work-in-progress commits before review, but merge (or squash-merge) into main through a pull request. Many teams on GitHub use 'Squash and Merge' which squashes all your feature branch commits into one clean commit on main — giving you the best of both worlds.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Merge: preserves true branching history, safe on shared branches, creates merge commits
Rebase: creates linear history, cleaner log, but rewrites commits — unsafe on shared branches
Common workflow: rebase locally to clean up, merge (or squash-merge) into main via PR
Never rebase: branches others are actively working from (main, develop, shared feature branches)
Squash and Merge (GitHub): squashes all feature commits into one — popular middle ground

questions.question: What is a merge conflict and what causes it?
questions.title: What Causes a Git Merge Conflict?
questions.direct_answer: A merge conflict occurs when two branches modify the same line(s) of the same file differently, and Git cannot automatically determine which version to keep.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical experience with Git and understanding of what conflicts mean
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Panicking at merge conflicts — they're normal and easy to resolve once you understand them
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that some conflicts are in content while others are structural (one branch deletes a file the other modifies)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A merge conflict happens when two developers edit the same part of the same file on different branches, and Git doesn't know which version to keep when you try to merge. Git is actually quite smart — it can automatically merge changes when they're in different parts of a file. Conflicts only arise when both branches touched the same lines. For example, I edit line 10 of UserService.java on my feature branch to add a null check. Meanwhile, my colleague edits that same line on their branch to refactor the method name. When we try to merge, Git marks the file as conflicted and inserts conflict markers. Another type of conflict is when one branch deletes a file that the other branch modified — Git doesn't know whether to keep the modification or respect the deletion. Conflicts are completely normal in team development — the key is knowing how to recognize them (git status will list conflicted files) and resolve them carefully.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Conflicts occur when two branches modify the same lines of the same file
Git can auto-merge changes in different parts of a file — conflicts only occur on the same lines
Another conflict type: one branch deletes a file that the other branch modified
'git status' shows which files have conflicts after a failed merge
Conflicts are normal — they're resolved by manually editing the file and committing

questions.question: What is the golden rule of git rebase?
questions.title: The Golden Rule of Git Rebase
questions.direct_answer: Never rebase commits that exist on a public or shared branch — because rebase rewrites commit hashes, it causes divergent history for anyone else who has pulled those commits.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the danger of rebase on shared branches — a key team safety concern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Rebasing main or develop after others have pulled from it, causing history divergence for the whole team
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what actually happens technically — new commit SHA hashes are created — and why that breaks other developers' repos

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The golden rule is: never rebase commits that already exist on a shared or public branch. Here's why. When you rebase, Git doesn't move your existing commits — it creates brand new commit objects with new SHA-1 hashes. Your original commits are abandoned and replaced with new ones that have identical content but different identities. Now imagine you've pushed your feature branch to origin and a colleague has pulled it and is working on top of it. If you rebase that branch, your copies and their copies of the 'same' commits now have different SHA hashes. When they try to pull or merge, Git sees two different lines of history and it gets very messy — they'll have duplicate commits and a confusing state. Safe zones for rebase: your own local feature branch that hasn't been pushed, or a feature branch you pushed but you're the only one using. Unsafe: main, develop, release branches, or any feature branch others have branched from or are working on.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Never rebase commits that are on a public or shared branch
Rebase creates new commit objects with new SHA hashes — it's a rewrite of history
If others have pulled the original commits, their history diverges from yours after a rebase
Safe to rebase: local-only branches, or private feature branches you haven't shared
If you accidentally push a rebased branch, use 'git push --force-with-lease' (with caution and team communication)
